'''Nancy Beth Jackson''' (March 1, 1956 – January 3, 2022) was an American chemist. She did energy research on [[heterogeneous catalysis]] and the development of [[alternative fuels]].<ref name=Rochester>{{cite web|title=Dr. Nancy B. Jackson, President ACS, Distinguished Speaker Series|url=http://www.rit.edu/cos/Nancy_Jackson|website=Rochester Institute of Technology|access-date=September 18, 2015}}</ref>  She also worked in the field of chemical nonproliferation, educating chemical professionals on the importance of safe and secure chemical practice in research, teaching and business, in an effort to prevent the misuse of chemicals as "weapons, poisons, explosives or environmental pollutants".<ref name=Rochester/><ref name=Stoesser/> She was the first implementer in developing the international Chemical Security Engagement Program.<ref name=AAAS/><ref name=Launch>{{cite web|title=Nancy Jackson|url=http://www.launch.org/council/nancy-jackson|website=Launch|access-date=October 1, 2015}}</ref><ref name=FFA>{{cite web|title=Dr. Nancy Jackson|url=https://careers.state.gov/ff/meet-the-fellows/franklin-fellows/dr_-nancy-jackson|website=Franklin Fellows Alumni|publisher=U. S. Department of State|access-date=October 1, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151002125406/https://careers.state.gov/ff/meet-the-fellows/franklin-fellows/dr_-nancy-jackson|archive-date=October 2, 2015|url-status=dead}}</ref> She was active in promoting diversity in [[STEM fields]].<ref name=Seneca>{{cite web|title=Native American Heritage Month 2014: Nancy B. Jackson|url=https://2009-2017.state.gov/r/pa/ei/pix/nahm/2014/233519.htm|access-date=September 18, 2015|website=U. S. Department of State|date=November 1, 2014}}</ref> She was president of the [[American Chemical Society]] in 2011, leading the organization during the [[International Year of Chemistry]].<ref name=Stoesser/><ref name=Raber>{{cite news|last1=Raber|first1=Linda R.|title=Nancy Jackson Wins ACS Presidential Race|url=http://cen.acs.org/articles/87/web/2009/11/Nancy-Jackson-Wins-ACS-Presidential.html?type=paidArticleContent|access-date=September 19, 2015|work=Chemical & Engineering News|date=November 18, 2009}}</ref> In 2012, she was honored with the [[AAAS Award for Science Diplomacy]].<ref name=AAAS/>

==Early life and education==
Jackson was born March 1, 1956, in [[Eau Claire, Wisconsin]], to a [[Seneca people|Seneca]] father and a white mother. Both of her parents were ministers, and both of her grandmothers held master's degrees.<ref name=SACNAS/> One of her grandfathers came from the [[Cattaraugus Reservation]] in upstate New York.<ref name=Seneca/>

Jackson initially studied [[political science]] at university, but became increasingly interested in science.<ref name=SACNAS>{{cite web|last1=Jackson|first1=Nancy|title=Dr. Nancy Jackson – Chemist|url=http://bio.sacnas.org/beta/pdf/jacksonhs.pdf|website=SACNAS Biography Project|access-date=September 18, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304110938/http://bio.sacnas.org/beta/pdf/jacksonhs.pdf|archive-date=March 4, 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref>  She received a B.S. in chemistry from [[George Washington University]] in 1979.<ref name=President-Elect/> After working briefly in the education department of the American Chemical Society she decided to return to school at the [[University of Texas at Austin]]. She received an  M.S. in chemical engineering in 1986 and a Ph.D. in chemical engineering in 1990, working in the area of [[catalysis]].<ref name=President-Elect/>

==Career==
Jackson joined the Catalysis and Chemical Technologies department of the Energy and Environment sector at [[Sandia National Laboratories]] in [[Albuquerque, New Mexico]], in 1991.<ref name=President-Elect/>  There she worked as an energy researcher for many years, focusing on alternative energy sources such as [[solar fuel]].<ref name=Rochester/> She has studied [[heterogeneous catalysis]] with an emphasis on identifying catalysts that can enable production of liquid fuels from non-petroleum sources.<ref name=Cornerstone>{{cite web|title=Nancy Jackson Senior Member of Technical Staff Sandia National Laboratories Albuquerque, NM|url=http://www.careercornerstone.org/chemistry/profiles/jackson.htm|website=Profiles of Chemists|publisher=Career Cornerstone Center|access-date=September 18, 2015}}</ref> In addition, she became an associate research professor in the Department of Chemical and Nuclear Engineering of the [[University of New Mexico]] in 1999.<ref name=President-Elect>{{cite journal|title=ACS Elections: Candidates' Election Statements And Backgrounds For President-Elect: Nancy B. Jackson|journal=Chemical & Engineering News|volume=87|issue=36|pages=75–76|url=https://pubs.acs.org/cen/acsnews/87/8736electionC1.html|access-date=September 7, 2009|doi=10.1021/cen-v087n036.p075|year=2009|doi-access=free}}</ref>

Jackson was manager of the Chemical and Biological Imaging, Sensing and Analysis Department at Sandia from 2000–2004.<ref name=President-Elect/> Her work involved chemical imaging techniques including fluorescent and infrared imaging, point infrared spectroscopy, and analysis of hyperspectral images and materials.  Applications included imaging of DNA microarrays, analysis of polymeric materials, and examination of the structure-property relationships of heterogeneous catalytic materials.<ref name=NAP>{{cite book|title=Visualizing Chemistry: The Progress and Promise of Advanced Chemical Imaging|date=2006|publisher=The National Academies Press|location=Washington, D.C.|page=200|doi=10.17226/11663|pmid=21977538|isbn=978-0-309-09722-2|url=http://www.nap.edu/read/11663/chapter/8|access-date=September 18, 2015|author1=National Research Council (US) Committee on Revealing Chemistry through Advanced Chemical Imaging}}</ref>

She was deputy director of the International Security Center at Sandia from 2004–2006.<ref name=President-Elect/>  In 2007, she became founder and manager of the International Chemical Threat Reduction Department in the Global Security Center at Sandia.<ref name=President-Elect/><ref name=CatalysisEnergy>{{cite book|last1=Catalysis Science Program, Committee on the Review of the Basic Energy Sciences, Board on Chemical Sciences and Technology, Division on Earth and Life Studies, National Research Council|title=Catalysis for Energy:: Fundamental Science and Long-Term Impacts of the U.S. Department of Energy Basic Energy Science Catalysis Science Program|publisher=National Academies Press|page=102|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4gaPTzXDyn4C&pg=PA102|access-date=March 9, 2009|isbn=9780309177467|date=March 9, 2009}}</ref> Jackson was the first implementer to work with the [[United States Department of State|U.S. Department of State]] to develop the Chemical Security Engagement Program, an international program to raise awareness about chemical safety and security among chemical professionals throughout Southeast Asia, South Asia, the Middle East, and North Africa. As part of her work she has traveled extensively in these areas.<ref name=CHFVoice>{{cite web|title=I'm seeing women gain power in the scientific community|url=http://www.chemheritage.org/discover/online-resources/stories-from-the-field/nancy-jackson.aspx|website=Chemical Heritage Foundation|url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160712165241/http://www.chemheritage.org/discover/online-resources/stories-from-the-field/nancy-jackson.aspx|archive-date=July 12, 2016}}</ref><ref name=Fellows>{{cite web|title=Meet the Fellows|url=http://careers.state.gov/work/fellowships/franklin-fellows/meet|website=U.S. Department of State|access-date=September 18, 2015|archive-date=September 5, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150905223418/http://careers.state.gov/work/fellowships/franklin-fellows/meet|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Jackson was active in encouraging diversity in [[STEM fields|STEM]]. She was Seneca, and was a member of the American Indian Science and Engineering Society. She has served as a tribal government liaison for Sandia, and worked with tribal colleges in developing the Science and Technology Alliance, a STEM program for underrepresented minorities.<ref name=Seneca/> She is also an active advocate for women in STEM fields.<ref name=Coyle>{{cite news|last1=Coyle|first1=Joan|title=Women Chemists Committee announces inaugural Rising Star Award and winners|url=http://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/pressroom/newsreleases/2011/december/women-chemists-committee-announces-inaugural-rising-star-award-and-winners.html|access-date=September 18, 2015|work=ACS News Release|agency=American Chemical Society|date=December 1, 2011}}</ref><ref name=Krapfl>{{cite news|last1=Krapfl|first1=Mike|title=Iowa State researcher among the first class of women rising stars of chemistry|url=http://www.news.iastate.edu/news/2011/dec/risingstaraward|access-date=September 18, 2015|work=Iowa State University|date=December 13, 2011}}</ref><ref name=PowerMore>{{cite web|last1=Johnson|first1=Sandra K.|title=Women in tech: Meet the trailblazers of STEM equality|url=https://powermore.dell.com/business/women-in-tech-meet-the-trailblazers-of-stem-equality/|website=Power More|access-date=September 18, 2015|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150501072201/https://powermore.dell.com/business/women-in-tech-meet-the-trailblazers-of-stem-equality/|archive-date=May 1, 2015}}</ref>

Jackson was a Fellow of the [[American Chemical Society]], the [[International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry]], and the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]]. She was elected in 2009 to the presidential succession of the American Chemical Society, serving as president-elect in 2010, president during the United Nations' [[International Year of Chemistry]] in 2011,<ref name=Welcome>{{cite journal|last1=Jackson|first1=Nancy B.|title=Welcome To The International Year Of Chemistry!|url=http://cen.acs.org/articles/89/i1/Welcome-International-Year-Chemistry.html|access-date=September 19, 2015|journal=Chemical & Engineering News|volume=89|number=1|pages=2–4|date=January 3, 2011|doi=10.1021/cen-v089n001.p002|url-access=subscription}}</ref> and immediate past president in 2012.<ref name=Stoesser>{{cite web |title=2014-15 Sylvia M. Stoesser Lecture in Chemistry Nancy B. Jackson |url=https://chemistry.illinois.edu/2014-15-sylvia-m-stoesser-lecture-chemistry |website=University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign |access-date=June 27, 2019}}</ref> During the three-year period following her election, she focused on expanding international collaboration, visiting more than 20 countries on five continents to meet with chemists and chemical engineers, many of them women.<ref name=Franklin/>

In 2012, she received the [[AAAS Award for Science Diplomacy]]<ref name=Pinholster>{{cite web|last1=Pinholster|first1=Ginger|title=Nancy B. Jackson, Chemical Security Leader, Wins 2012 AAAS Award for Science Diplomacy|url=http://www.aaas.org/news/nancy-b-jackson-chemical-security-leader-wins-2012-aaas-award-science-diplomacy|access-date=September 19, 2015|website=AAAS Advancing Science, Serving Society|publisher=American Association for the Advancement of Science|date=December 18, 2012}}</ref>   "for her ongoing commitment to international science cooperation to prevent the theft and diversion of chemicals through the establishment of the Chemical Security Engagement Program and for developing, nurturing, and advancing careers of scientists worldwide, with a special emphasis on women scientists in the Middle East and Southeast Asia."<ref name=AAAS>{{cite web|title=AAAS Award for Science Diplomacy: Recipients|url=http://www.aaas.org/page/aaas-award-science-diplomacy-recipients|website=AAAS Advancing Science, Serving Society|publisher=American Association for the Advancement of Science|access-date=September 18, 2015}}</ref>

In 2014, she became the 174th Franklin Fellow at the U.S. Department of State.<ref name=Franklin>{{cite web|title=Franklin Fellows Alumni|url=https://careers.state.gov/ff/alumni|website=U. S. Department of State|access-date=September 18, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151005081821/https://careers.state.gov/ff/alumni|archive-date=October 5, 2015|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Personal life and death==
She died in Albuquerque, New Mexico, on January 3, 2022, at the age of 65. She was survived by her husband and their two sons.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://cen.acs.org/people/obituaries/Nancy-B-Jackson-former-president/100/web/2022/01|title=Nancy B. Jackson, former president of the American Chemical Society, dies at 65|work=[[Chemical & Engineering News]]|first=Alexandra|last=Taylor|date=January 10, 2022|access-date=January 10, 2022}}</ref>

==Awards and honors==
* 2014–15 [[Sylvia M. Stoesser Lecturer in Chemistry]] at the University of Illinois<ref name=Stoesser/>
* 2012, [[AAAS Award for Science Diplomacy]].<ref name=AAAS/><ref name=Pinholster/>
* 2011,  President of the American Chemical Society<ref name=Raber/>
* 2011, Distinguished Women in Chemistry and Chemical Engineering Award, International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry<ref name=Pillitteri>{{cite news|last1=Pillitteri|first1=Abigail|last2=Rousseaux|first2=Charles|title=They Have Chemistry DOE researchers among those recognized as world's most distinguished|url=http://science.energy.gov/news/featured-articles/2011/06-27-11/|access-date=September 18, 2015|work=SC News|date=June 27, 2011}}</ref>
* 2009, Howard Fawcett Chemical Health & Safety Award<ref name=Pinholster/>
* 2005, [[American Indian Science and Engineering Society]] (AISES) Professional of the Year award.<ref name=CHFVoice/>
* 2005, Distinguished Alumni Achievement Award, [[George Washington University]]<ref name=Nehmer>{{cite news|last1=Nehmer|first1=Matthew|title=GW PRESIDENT STEPHEN JOEL TRACHTENBERG AND THE GW ALUMNI ASSOCIATION ANNOUNCE RECIPIENTS OF 68th ANNUAL DISTINGUISHED ALUMNI ACHIEVEMENT AWARDS|url=http://www.gwu.edu/~media/pressrelease.cfm?ann_id=11442|access-date=September 19, 2015|work=George Washington University Office of University Relations|date=April 8, 2004}}</ref>
